entities.name: Flavian dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Flavian dynasty (69-96 CE), founded by Vespasian after the Year of the Four Emperors (69 CE) — the chaotic year when four men claimed the Roman Empire in succession (Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian) following Nero's suicide — ruled Rome for 27 years through three emperors: Vespasian (69-79 CE), Titus (79-81 CE), and Domitian (81-96 CE). Despite its short duration, the Flavian dynasty accomplished the greatest construction project in Roman history (the Colosseum), suppressed the Jewish Revolt with the destruction of Jerusalem (70 CE), and survived the Vesuvius eruption (79 CE) that destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum.

Vespasian (r. 69-79 CE) was a practical, frugal emperor who restored financial stability after the civil wars and began construction of the Flavian Amphitheatre (Colosseum); his son Titus completed it. The Colosseum — completed 80 CE and inaugurated with 100 days of games — remains the world's most iconic ancient building and the architectural symbol of Rome. Titus's brief reign (79-81 CE) was marked by the Vesuvius eruption (August 24, 79 CE) that buried Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Stabiae — preserving a snapshot of Roman urban life that has shaped archaeology and our understanding of ancient Rome.

Domitian (81-96 CE) — Titus's younger brother — ruled increasingly autocratically, claiming the title 'dominus et deus' ('lord and god'), persecuting senators and Christians, and was assassinated by his own court officials in 96 CE. His assassination inaugurated the reign of the Five Good Emperors (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius) — considered Rome's golden age — making the Flavian dynasty the transition between the troubled Julio-Claudians and Rome's imperial peak.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Flavian dynasty — building the Colosseum (world's most iconic ancient monument), presiding over Pompeii's destruction that preserved the best Roman urban site, and destroying Jerusalem's Temple in 70 CE — created three of antiquity's most consequential physical legacies in just 27 years.
